response.translation: But since, as wickedness increased over time, there was no longer anything either undared or [324] unsaid among human beings, the lawgivers devised many new modes of punishment for wrongdoers, while those who honour truth devised manifold forms of refutation against the sophists — which is what we too now seem likely to do, refuting those who abolish the attractive power of purgative drugs over the humours which they evacuate, and assert that they possess a certain transformative power over all things alike that come into contact with them. raw_text: {"translation": "And the power in purgative drugs is a part of the power that attracts what is proper to it, [325] just as is also that by which the bile is separated off, and the urine, and many other things that are brought about by nature in the health of animals, and in the cures of diseases and in the diseases themselves, both by physicians and, not least, by nature itself. Since, then, Hippocrates said nothing against those who abolish attraction from among the things that exist, because the doctrine did not yet have so brazen a champion as many of those after them became, it would be just for us to contend for the truth in Hippocrates' place, and first to recall what sort of thing these men say, and then next to show that they do not speak correctly. Their argument, then, is as follows. raw_text: {"translation": "[326] To put it briefly, what is called purgation is, according to their account, a change and alteration of all the humours in the veins, not an evacuation of one of them. But if this is what you want, let us now say to them that whether someone takes a drug that draws bile, or phlegm, or black bile, or serous moisture, all the humours from the veins are evacuated. And indeed, purging someone with such a drug would then differ in this respect only from evacuating the blood by cutting a vein, inasmuch as in phlebotomies it is excreted such as it was present before, whereas in purgations it is altered not only in colour but also in consistency. For the drug that draws watery humours makes everything in the veins fluid and thin, even if it happened to be very thick before; while that which draws black bile, conversely, makes everything thick and stagnant, even if before it was very fluid. And accordingly, our choice between phlebotomizing and purging will be made according to certain other indications, but will not be made according to the very kind of the things evacuated. raw_text: {"translation": "[329] But this we have demonstrated not once or twice, but very many times, to the half-wicked among them, and many we have converted to better views. raw_text: {"translation": "But you, if you think that all are altered alike [331] and that what happens is a common evacuation, not a purgation, are free to cut the vein. response.translation: For a whole day I could go on recounting still other [342] marvellous effects that follow upon purgings, of which it is natural that those who have never learned the art concerning purgative drugs should be ignorant. For where they do not even think that there exists any purgative drug at all, how indeed will they know in which cases one must use it, or in what manner? For this reason some treat the affections guided by bare and sole experience; but these wise men of ours, who take reason too in hand, not so as to add anything to what has been discovered through experience, but so as to overturn even this, practise medicine far worse than those who set out from bare and sole irrational routines. Of all these things there is one origin and source, the hatred toward Hippocrates, from which source there have flowed many other things, and also this very inquiry now before us, that concerning the attractive power, of which the power of purgative drugs is a part, or a species, or whatever one might wish to call it.
